items.headline: BRICS countries adopt New Delhi Declaration
items.gist: The New Delhi declaration called for comprehensive reform of the United Nations, including support for Brazil and India to get a bigger role in the Security Council, and expressed deep concern over attacks on civilian infrastructure and nuclear facilities in West Asia. Prime Minister Narendra Modi said BRICS was "coming of age" with a distinct identity not aimed against others, proposed a troika system like the G-20, a road map for global governance reform, a seafarer distress network, and a BRICS global south mechanism for skill development in new technologies.
items.paragraph: The New Delhi declaration called for comprehensive reform of the United Nations, including support for Brazil and India to get a bigger role in the Security Council, and expressed deep concern over attacks on civilian infrastructure and nuclear facilities in West Asia. Prime Minister Narendra Modi said BRICS was "coming of age" with a distinct identity not aimed against others, proposed a troika system like the G-20, a road map for global governance reform, a seafarer distress network, and a BRICS global south mechanism for skill development in new technologies. Chinese President Xi Jinping, who held an hour-long bilateral with Mr. Modi after the session, announced China would take over the BRICS presidency for the next year; the declaration also criticised the U.S. blockade of Cuba and expressed concern over violence in Sudan. Consensus on West Asia language was achieved through months of threadbare discussions after Iran sought strong condemnation of U.S. and Israel strikes and the UAE wanted equal condemnation of Iran's attacks, with Indian Sherpa Sudhakar Dalela saying cooperation of all members was key; BRICS countries also underscored consensus against cross-border terrorism, with specific reference to the Pahalgam terror attack in 2025.

items.headline: Saudi Arabia closes key oil pipeline after strikes
items.gist: Threatening to send energy prices even higher amid the war in West Asia, Saudi Arabia has shut down its 1,200-kilometre-long East-West pipeline after the vital oil conduit came under aerial attack, with the kingdom saying the attack originated in Iraq where Iran-backed militias operate. The pipeline, used by Riyadh as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, has been moving close to 5 million barrels of oil per day in recent months, amounting to 5% of global supply.

The pipeline, used by Riyadh as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, has been moving close to 5 million barrels of oil per day in recent months, amounting to 5% of global supply. The Saudi Arabian Foreign Ministry said the attack resulted in some injuries and damage that was being assessed; though an umbrella group of Iran-backed militias in Iraq denied involvement, Iraq's government said the attacks originated from its territory, pledged a probe, and dismissed two senior officials, AP reported.

items.headline: Trump stirs Irish stew, risks souring British ties
items.gist: During a visit to Ireland on Saturday, President Donald Trump told Taoiseach Micheal Martin he would "love to see" Irish reunification happen now rather than eventually, calling it "a fantastic thing" while noting "The UK will have something to say about it, obviously." The remarks sent ripples through Northern Ireland, where unionist politicians stressed the province's constitutional future is for its people to decide under the Good Friday Agreement, and analysts warned similar unpredictable pronouncements could unsettle diplomacy on issues from Korea to Taiwan.

items.headline: England complete 3-0 sweep of Pak
items.gist: England beat Pakistan by eight wickets at Edgbaston on Saturday to seal a 3-0 Test series sweep, chasing 130 after losing both openers in the first over to Mohammad Abbas. Joe Root was unbeaten on 62 and Jordan Cox 59 not out, though England had floundered on Friday when debutant Razaullah raced to 81 off 63 balls with nine sixes and added 121 for the ninth wicket with Abbas (42); Pakistan had already lost the first two Tests by an innings and 103 runs and by 194 runs, sacked coaches Sarfaraz Ahmed and Umar Gul, and sent seven players home after Lord’s.

items.gist: Hull City held Chelsea 2-2 at Stamford Bridge as Liverpool drew 0-0 with Fulham in Premier League action on Saturday. items.headline: Revisiting the feminist icon
items.gist: Aisiri Amin recalls Gloria Steinem’s death at 92, tracing her Ohio childhood, two years in India on the Charles Bowles Fellowship including time at Delhi University’s Miranda House, 1963 undercover reporting on Hugh Hefner’s Playboy Club, co-founding *Ms Magazine* in 1971, and landmark feminist advocacy. Amin also notes criticism that Steinem catered to educated white women, her CIA-linked Independent Research Service work, 1998 defence of Bill Clinton, evolving 2013 support for transgender people, and her 1958 sari advertisement image from the Gloria Steinem Foundation archives.

items.headline: Courage to refuse
items.gist: Chintan Girish Modi profiles Ella Keidar Greenberg, imprisoned in March 2025 as the first openly transgender conscientious objector in Israel since Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack, and Aiden Katri, who refused enlistment in 2016 citing apartheid against Palestinians. He links their “refusenik” tradition to resistance against compulsory military service and “pinkwashing,” quoting Ella’s pledge that she would tell future grandchildren she chose to resist during the genocide.

items.headline: BRICS bold stand: 'Enough' in Mideast
items.gist: The BRICS group unanimously adopted a joint declaration at its two-day New Delhi summit hosted by PM Modi, calling for calm in the Middle East and stressing cooperation to maintain global trade, supply chains and energy flows. The declaration voiced deep concern over escalating tensions, called for maximum restraint, warned against attacks on civilian infrastructure and safeguarded nuclear facilities, and reiterated support for Palestine including full UN membership.

items.headline: Iran President, Abu Dhabi Crown Prince discuss regional hostilities
items.gist: Against the backdrop of continued hostilities in West Asia, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan held talks in New Delhi on Saturday on the sidelines of the 18th BRICS Summit, discussing regional hostilities and expressing support for de-escalation. The conversation came ten days after Iran targeted military installations in the United Arab Emirates; the New Delhi Declaration expressed deep concern about multiple West Asia conflicts but stopped short of naming major stakeholders.
items.paragraph: Against the backdrop of continued hostilities in West Asia, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan held talks in New Delhi on Saturday on the sidelines of the 18th BRICS Summit, discussing regional hostilities and expressing support for de-escalation. The conversation came ten days after Iran targeted military installations in the United Arab Emirates; the New Delhi Declaration expressed deep concern about multiple West Asia conflicts but stopped short of naming major stakeholders. The Abu Dhabi Media Office said both leaders underscored the importance of easing tensions, promoting de-escalation and strengthening regional stability, while Iranian state outlet IRNA said the meeting followed Iran's emphasis on strengthening relations with its southern neighbours. Mr. Pezeshkian said West Asia does not need the United States, at war with Iran, to be a regional policeman, telling Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim that the region's territorial integrity and security can only be guaranteed by its main players. The declaration called for maximum restraint, maintaining smooth global trade and energy flows, halting policies aimed at forced displacement of Palestinians, support for a sovereign Palestinian state within 1967 borders with East Jerusalem as capital, Israel's obligation to supply humanitarian aid in Gaza, withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanese territories, and took a strong position on attacks on UNIFIL.

items.gist: Brazil's Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira praised India's BRICS presidency and said bilateral trade could exceed the $30 billion target well before 2030, adding it is not correct to view BRICS as an anti-West alliance. Following President Lula da Silva's February visit, Brazil and India are rapidly expanding trade past last year's $15 billion toward $20 billion, and Mr.
items.paragraph: Brazil's Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira praised India's BRICS presidency and said bilateral trade could exceed the $30 billion target well before 2030, adding it is not correct to view BRICS as an anti-West alliance. Following President Lula da Silva's February visit, Brazil and India are rapidly expanding trade past last year's $15 billion toward $20 billion, and Mr. Vieira said deals by Embraer, Vale, WEG and others could push trade above $30 billion in the short term. He highlighted the New Development Bank as a vital alternative to Bretton Woods institutions, said Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin's attendance underscores India's pivotal global role, and argued BRICS allows major regional powers with bilateral differences to engage informally; the group has entered a consolidation phase focused on integrating new members rather than further enlargement. Mr. Vieira said Brazil's foreign policy relies on peace, constitutional multilateralism and active diplomacy over military force, with President Lula expanding trade and political ties worldwide.

items.headline: Human drug use began millennia earlier than believed
items.gist: Researchers examined the teeth of two ancient hunter-gatherers from Sulawesi, Indonesia, dating back as far as 25,000 years, and found unusual deep grooves caused by sucking on betel nuts, with chemical analyses confirming the presence of arecoline, the main stimulant in betel nuts. The find suggests these early foragers habitually kept whole nuts in their mouths for long periods, pushing back the timeline of human drug use by thousands of years.

items.headline: Even Teflon may not stop water if the liquid is charged
items.gist: As water drops slide over leaves, glass or plastic, they develop an electric charge, and when such charged drops land on a metal surface, even one with a protective coating like Teflon, the charge creates an electric field strong enough to punch microscopic holes through the coating, allowing water to reach the metal below and leading to rust and decay. This new discovery shows a previously unrecognised way in which bridges, ships, cars, and heritage sites may degrade.

items.headline: The new lords of the Red Sea
items.gist: The Houthis seized Perim Island at the mouth of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in early September after Saudi-backed forces bombed Sana'a airport's runway to prevent an Iranian aircraft carrying a Houthi delegation from landing, breaking a 2022 ceasefire and triggering Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure including the shutdown of the East-West pipeline. Rooted in the Zaydi revivalist 'Believing Youth' movement founded in the early 1990s, the Houthis captured Sana'a in 2014, survived a Saudi-led bombing campaign from 2015, and have transformed into a formidable territorial and naval force with Iranian support, now controlling the Red Sea coastline and, together with Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz, exerting pressure on two of the world's critical maritime chokepoints through which more than 20% of seaborne oil trade and roughly 12-15% of global maritime trade typically pass.

items.headline: Alice Weidel
items.gist: Alice Weidel, co-leader of Germany's far-right Alternative für Deutschland, declared "Mr. Merz, your time has run out" after the party secured 43% of the vote in Saxony Anhalt, consolidating its position as a front-runner ahead of the 2029 federal elections.
items.paragraph: Alice Weidel, co-leader of Germany's far-right Alternative für Deutschland, declared "Mr. Merz, your time has run out" after the party secured 43% of the vote in Saxony Anhalt, consolidating its position as a front-runner ahead of the 2029 federal elections. A former Goldman Sachs analyst fluent in Mandarin who lived in China for nearly six years, Ms. Weidel is the AfD's first lesbian leader and is in a civil partnership with a German national of Sri Lankan origin with two adopted children, yet the party opposes same-sex marriage and emphasises Christian values and traditional families while campaigning against immigration from Muslim-majority countries. Her grandfather Hans Weidel was a Nazi party member and military judge, and Ms. Weidel has dismissed Germany's culture of remembrance over Nazi crimes as a "cult of guilt" even as she gains favour with a wider German electorate.

items.headline: 5 killed, dozens injured in Russian strikes on Ukraine
items.gist: Russian strikes killed five civilians and wounded dozens in Ukraine on Saturday, local officials said, after Russian President Vladimir Putin warned that sending European troops into Ukraine would amount to direct conflict with Russia. Moscow's intensifying air campaign targeted Ukraine's power grid ahead of winter, with attacks on Zaporizhzhia, Kryvyi Rih, Odesa and Zhytomyr region killing civilians and destroying a residential high-rise in Odesa where 35 people were wounded in what regional head Oleh Kiper called a "massive attack".

items.headline: Uganda buries 'youngest' king
items.gist: Several thousand people gathered on Saturday in Uganda to pay final respects to King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who ascended the throne at age three and reigned over the Tooro Kingdom for 31 years before dying at 34 while receiving cancer treatment in the United States. Guinness World Records had recognised him as the world's youngest reigning monarch, and President urged unity amid a dispute over succession at a burial ceremony at Saint John's Cathedral in Fort Portal, where his sister Princess Ruth Komuntale said he "had a gift to make people laugh."

items.headline: It's an all-American Top 10 rich list as tech dominates
items.gist: French luxury goods tycoon Bernard Arnault fell out of the top 10 on the Bloomberg Billionaires Index as his net worth dropped to $143 billion, leaving an all-American roster of mostly tech billionaires to dominate the rankings for the first time since the index's 2012 launch. Elon Musk leads with a $918.8 billion fortune, followed by Larry Page, Jeff Bezos, Sergey Brin and Michael Dell, while Arnault fell below Warren Buffett's $143 billion.

items.headline: Al-Qaida, terror training camps back in Af: US
items.gist: Al-Qaida and terrorist training camps are back in Afghanistan 25 years after 9/11, with the Washington Post reporting at least eight training sites established over the past three years exploiting the security vacuum after the Taliban's return and the 2021 US withdrawal. UN monitors and Western intelligence officials say the camps cover weapons, explosives, guerrilla warfare and instruction involving encryption, drones and AI, with militant Islamist groups now present in at least 14 of Afghanistan's 34 provinces; the report notes al-Qaida's current leader Saif al-Adel is believed to be hiding in Iran and revisits Pakistan's historical role in the network's South Asia operations.

items.headline: Capgemini sells subsidiary after row over ICE ties
items.gist: French IT giant Capgemini said on Saturday it was selling its US subsidiary Capgemini Government Solutions to ITC Federal after the unit came under pressure for its work for US Immigration and Customs Enforcement amid nationwide backlash over ICE's aggressive tactics in enforcing President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown. The subsidiary represented 0.4% of the group's global 2025 revenue and less than 2% of its US revenue.

items.headline: Zelensky ready to meet Putin at G20
items.gist: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he would be willing to meet Russian leader Vladimir Putin at the G20 summit in Miami on Dec 14-15 for talks on ending more than four years of war, telling Deutsche Welle that leaders "have to meet, to speak, and make decisions" because only "results" matter. The Kremlin said it had not decided whether Putin would attend and repeated his demand that Zelensky come to Russia for talks, as US negotiators visit Kyiv and Moscow to restart stalled peace efforts.

items.headline: Toll in Philippines ferry fire rises to 76; 13 missing
items.gist: Philippine rescuers recovered 41 more charred remains from a ferry fire on Saturday, raising the death toll to 76 with 13 people unaccounted for after the vessel caught fire on Wednesday en route from Manila to Palawan. Forensic teams set up temporary tents in Coron town to identify victims, with the Coast Guard finding burnt remains in the economy accommodation section and the Maritime Industry Authority citing survivor accounts of two explosions shortly before the fire broke out.

items.headline: Tunisia reports prison deaths due to heatwave
items.gist: At least 23 prisoners have died in Tunisia in recent weeks due to extreme heat, according to rights advocates, though authorities have not released official summer prison-death figures and said no death can be attributed to heat without forensic confirmation. The Tunisian League for Human Rights documented the 23 deaths based on information from doctors, lawyers and relatives of prisoners who died in jail from the heat.

items.headline: Egyptians budget for bread after mass food aid cuts
items.gist: Eman Abdel Fattah, a 42-year-old Cairo mother of four, said her family now worries about affording bread after their food subsidy card was suspended in July, with flatbread costing 10 times more than before. She is among 850,000 people removed from Egypt's subsidy system since June as part of IMF-backed reforms that will reportedly exclude millions more next year, in a country where a third of Egyptians lived below the poverty line before the 2022 economic crisis.

items.headline: Chinese readout quotes Modi as saying ties with Beijing not influenced by any country
items.gist: PM Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping held a 40-minute bilateral on the BRICS summit margins in New Delhi—their third meeting in two years after Kazan (2024) and Tianjin, and the first on Indian soil in seven years. India’s readout cited commitment to border resolution and addressing trade deficit and supply-chain concerns; a Chinese readout quoted Modi as saying India follows an independent foreign policy and ties with Beijing are not influenced by any third country, and that India’s Taiwan and Tibet positions are unchanged.

items.headline: Modi proposes emergency seafarers support network
items.gist: Addressing the BRICS summit, PM Modi called for UNSC reform with text-based negotiations tied to a fixed timeline, greater voting power for growth-driving economies in global financial institutions, and a BRICS Continuity and Implementation Mechanism via the troika to sustain institutional momentum across rotating presidencies. He proposed a Seafarers Emergency Support Network linking maritime authorities and missions for distress alerts, medical aid, family notifications and evacuations, and said the Global South must move from “rule-takers to rule-shapers.” Modi said BRICS operates with an inclusive approach, not against anyone, as the bloc marks 20 years on the global stage.

items.headline: Don't agree with all his views, says Anwar Ibrahim on eve of meet with Kerala cleric
items.gist: Malaysian PM Anwar Ibrahim, ahead of a Sunday visit to Kozhikode to meet All-India Sunni Jemiyyathul Ulema general secretary Kanthapuram A P Aboobacker Musaliyar, told NDTV he does not agree with every view of the cleric, whose recent call for women to stay confined to homes drew backlash. Ibrahim called Kanthapuram a traditional Islamic scholar who also runs a college for women, but said in Malaysia women have equal rights, with more female university students and his wife a doctor.

items.headline: Snoop to make VMAs comeback
items.gist: Snoop Dogg will host the 2026 Video Music Awards at Peacock Theatre in Los Angeles on September 27, marking the ceremony’s return to the West Coast since 2017. The rapper, nominated 13 times and a three-time winner who debuted at the VMAs in 1994, said hosting completes a “full-circle moment” after MTV helped give hip hop “a place to be fearless and seen by the whole world.”

items.headline: Diana's iconic revenge dress is up for auction
items.gist: Princess Diana’s black silk “revenge dress” will be auctioned at Sotheby’s New York on December 9, with an estimate of $150,000 to $300,000 (₹1.4 to 2.8 crore). Designed by Christina Stambolian, the off-the-shoulder gown was worn to a Vanity Fair gala in London on June 29, 1994—the same evening King Charles III, then her husband, publicly admitted to infidelity—and became a symbol of her confidence and independence.

items.headline: Drones light up NYC harbour to recreate Twin Towers on 25th anniversary of 9/11
items.gist: The skies above New York Harbour became a moving tribute on Wednesday ahead of the 25th anniversary of September 11, in an artwork titled “2,977 Lights Over New York Harbor.” According to AP, 2,977 synchronised drone lights memorialised every life lost in the 9/11 attacks, and at one point the lights joined to recreate the Twin Towers at full architectural scale as they stood before the 2001 attacks.

items.headline: Hockey India strips Director General Srivastava of all powers
items.gist: Hockey India Director General Cdr. R.K.
items.paragraph: Hockey India Director General Cdr. R.K. Srivastava was divested of all authority and responsibilities and served notice to explain repeated instances of non-compliance with presidential directives, including travelling to recent World Cups in the Netherlands and Belgium despite explicit directions from president Dilip Tirkey against it. The legal notice mentions arbitrary decisions on changing the national team's jersey without prior consultation and non-availability of POSH committee proceedings among other charges, with Srivastava asked to reply within four weeks with documentary evidence.

items.headline: WUSHU PLAYER ALLEGES HARASSMENT AFTER GAMES AXE, FEDERATION CITES ACL TEAR
items.gist: Wushu player Divyanshi Choudhary has alleged she was dropped from India’s Asian Games squad to accommodate Roshibina Devi Naorem and accused the Wushu Association of India of physical and mental harassment, while the federation says her exclusion followed an MRI showing a high-grade ACL tear with large effusion. Divyanshi, who beat Roshibina in 60kg sanda selection trials, claimed mistreatment since June and threatened suicide in a video recorded on the NIS Patiala terrace; she attended the IOA send-off on September 8.

items.headline: Isharani in title round
items.gist: Isharani Baruah defeated compatriot Rakshitha Sree Santhosh Ramraj 21-10, 21-18 to reach the women’s singles final of the Vietnam Open Super 100 in Ho Chi Minh City on Saturday. Top seed Tanvi Sharma lost 19-21, 20-22 to unseeded Sarunrak Vitidsarn of Thailand, and HS Prannoy fell 13-21, 8-21 to top seed Jia Heng Teh of Singapore in the men’s singles semi-final.

items.headline: Red-hot Shelton downs Tiafoe
items.gist: Eighth seed Ben Shelton beat compatriot Frances Tiafoe 4-6, 6-3, 6-3, 7-5 with 20 aces at the US Open on Friday to reach his first Grand Slam final against Alexander Zverev, who defeated Karen Khachanov 6-3, 7-6 (9/7), 7-6 (8/6). Shelton, who eliminated defending champion Carlos Alcaraz in the quarterfinals, dedicated the win to his late grandmother and could become the first American men’s major champion since Andy Roddick in 2003.

items.headline: MAAYA & ANTONINA LOSE TO BIRTHDAY GIRLS IN SEMIFINALS
items.gist: India’s Maaya Rajeshwaran Revathi and Ukraine’s Antonina Sushkova lost to American twins Kristina and Annika Penickova 6-7 (3), 2-6 in the US Open girls’ doubles semi-finals in New York. The Indo-Ukrainian pair rallied from 2-5 to 5-5 and served for the opening set before the Penickovas forced a tie-break they won from 5-1, then broke in the first and fifth games of the second set.

items.headline: Norris takes pole
items.gist: Formula One championship leader Lando Norris pipped Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli to pole position for the Spanish Grand Prix at Madring on Saturday by just 11 thousandths of a second, with Max Verstappen qualifying third-fastest for Red Bull and Lewis Hamilton lining up next to Verstappen on the second row.

items.headline: Duplantis and Ingebrigtsen steal the show on first day
items.gist: Scandinavian stars Armand Duplantis and Jakob Ingebrigtsen shone on the opening day of the inaugural Ultimate Championship in Budapest, each walking away with $150,000 for winning the men's pole vault and 5,000m respectively at the $10 million event spanning 28 disciplines. Duplantis cleared 6.20 metres ahead of Greek rival Emmanouil Karalis while Norway's Ingebrigtsen clocked 12:59.24, and World record holders Masai Russell and Ja'Kobe Tharp won the short hurdles races.

items.headline: Supriya's hat-trick takes India to jr. women's Asia Cup final
items.gist: Drag-flick specialist Supriya put up a Player-of-the-Match show with a hat-trick as the Indian women's team entered the AHF junior Asia Cup hockey final, downing South Korea 5-1 in the semifinal at Moqi, China, on Saturday. items.headline: Sabalenka, Rybakina to meet in US Open final between top two players
items.gist: Aryna Sabalenka seeks a third consecutive US Open title against Elena Rybakina, who will become world No 1 on Monday regardless of the result after beating Coco Gauff in the semifinals. Sabalenka has lost only one set in six Flushing Meadows matches this year; Rybakina won January's Australian Open final against Sabalenka for her second 2026 major.

items.gist: Taylor Townsend and Katerina Siniakova completed a career Grand Slam as a team by beating wild cards Ashlyn Krueger and Robin Montgomery for their first US Open doubles crown. Townsend said Siniakova helped her through a nervous start before they found their rhythm in the final.

items.headline: Razaullah's six-hitting debut caps Pak fightback
items.gist: Debutant No 9 batter Razaullah Khan's six-hitting helped Pakistan reach 449 on day three at Edgbaston for a 129-run lead, forcing a fourth day after the team had been expected to fold quickly against England's pace attack. England still needed 130 to complete a 3-0 series sweep.

items.headline: Sarthak wins despite last-row start
items.gist: Teenager Sarthak Chavan shrugged off jet lag and a last-row start to win the premier Super Sport 301-400cc Open race in the second round of the MRF Indian National Racing Challenge 2W at the Madras International Circuit on Saturday, taking advantage of leader Rahil Pillarisetty's retirement. Chennai teenager Rakshith Dave finished second and Bengaluru's Chiranth Vishwanath completed a Petronas TVS Racing podium sweep.

items.headline: 'Winning in T20s is all about who plays better cricket on the day'
items.gist: India skipper Harmanpreet Kaur expects a tough fight in Sunday's Asia Cup final against reigning champion Sri Lanka, saying the last time India played Sri Lanka they came up with solid plans and performances. India will look to Shafali Verma and Deepti Sharma, the tournament's leading run-scorer and joint leading wicket-taker respectively, in a clash between two unbeaten sides at the Dubai International Cricket Stadium, mindful of Sri Lanka's crushing eight-wicket defeat inflicted on India in the 2024 final.

items.headline: Flintoff stars as Australia-A romps to win against India-A
items.gist: Tess Flintoff's four-wicket burst flattened India-A women as they suffered a six-wicket loss against Australia-A in the first match of the T20 series in New Chandigarh. India-A was bowled out for 117 in 19 overs before Australia-A chased down the target with four wickets in hand in 14 overs.

items.headline: Skipper Shreyas at ease with coach Gambhir's working style
items.gist: Skipper Shreyas Iyer shed light on his evolving rapport with coach Gautam Gambhir, saying Gambhir builds confidence among players and that having worked with him at KKR, he knows how his mind works and what his approach will be. India starts the T20I series against Afghanistan on Sunday as clear favourite but will not want to rest on its laurels after a shock series defeat to Ireland in June in Shreyas' first assignment as full-time skipper.

items.headline: 'Onus on simple plans, proper execution against Sooryavanshi'
items.gist: Afghanistan skipper Ibrahim Zadran said Vaibhav Sooryavanshi is an amazing talent and that his team has knowledge of how to bowl to him from IPL experience and video analysis, with the onus on keeping plans simple and executing them properly. The 15-year-old southpaw may face a short-pitched examination from Naveen-ul-Haq and Fazalhaq Farooqi when India meets Afghanistan in a three-match T20I series hosted in Delhi, with Afghanistan playing 'home' ties in India for the first time against the Men in Blue.

items.headline: Ahead of Asian Games, India aims to flex muscle
items.gist: India will hope for no more deviations from convention as Shreyas Iyer and Co. look to enter the Asian Games in Japan in red-hot form after a maiden series victory as captain in Zimbabwe, where Vaibhav Sooryavanshi scored two half-centuries.
items.paragraph: India will hope for no more deviations from convention as Shreyas Iyer and Co. look to enter the Asian Games in Japan in red-hot form after a maiden series victory as captain in Zimbabwe, where Vaibhav Sooryavanshi scored two half-centuries. With a fit-again Jasprit Bumrah back at full tilt, India aims to flex muscle against Afghanistan under the new captain-coach combination of Ibrahim Zadran and Richard Pybus at the Arun Jaitley Stadium on Sunday.

items.headline: 'Important for Bumrah to get game time'
items.gist: India has picked Jasprit Bumrah for three T20Is against Afghanistan and the Asian Games despite previously preserving him in white-ball formats when no World Cup was around the corner, with skipper Shreyas Iyer saying the idea is to give the spearhead, returning from a knee injury suffered during the England series, as much game time and confidence as possible ahead of next year's ODI World Cup. items.headline: Nepal seals Asia Cup 2027 berth after win over UAE
items.gist: Nepal secured a place in next year's Asia Cup with a 44-run win over the UAE in the ACC men's Premier Cup at the Bayuemas Oval in Kuala Lumpur, posting 313/9 before restricting the UAE to 269. This will be Nepal's second appearance in the continental tournament following its debut in 2023 in Sri Lanka, with Aasif Sheikh named Player-of-the-Match and Sandeep Lamichhane Player-of-the-Series.

items.headline: READY FOR THE BIG APPLE BITE
items.gist: Battle-hardened top seed Alexander Zverev beat Karen Khachanov 6-3, 7-6 (7), 7-6 (6) to reach his sixth Grand Slam final and third of 2026, and will face American Ben Shelton in Sunday’s US Open title match after Shelton defeated Frances Tiafoe 4-6, 6-3, 6-3, 7-5. Zverev, who broke a major drought at Roland Garros in June, hopes to add the US Open crown to his first Slam title and says he is ready for a sold-out Arthur Ashe Stadium crowd backing the home player.

items.headline: The First Black Man To Play In The US Open Final Since 1972 Is Not Overwhelmed By The Occasion
items.gist: Ben Shelton will become the first Black man to contest a US Open final since 1972 while chasing the first Queens title by an American man since Andy Roddick in 2003 and the first by a Black man since Arthur Ashe in 1968, yet the 23-year-old says he wants to cherish the moment without letting it overwhelm his tennis. Shelton, coached by his father Bryan Shelton, says he is a different player with more tools and is the most confident he has ever been despite trailing Alexander Zverev 5-0 in their head-to-head.

items.headline: 'High-flyer' Sehrawat ready to soar again
items.gist: Kabaddi star Pawan Sehrawat, nicknamed ‘High-flyer’ for his lion jumps and raiding, remains a vital cog as India chase another Asian Games gold after he captained the team to victory over Iran at Hangzhou 2022. Now deputy to captain Sunil Kumar, the 30-year-old from Bawana says the hunger to hear the national anthem on the podium is present in every player, and that India’s eight-to-nine-month preparation includes a video analyst in an “advanced approach.”

items.headline: GRAPPLING WITH LEGACY
items.gist: From Manila 1954 to Hangzhou 2022, Indian wrestlers built a proud Asian Games record of 65 medals since 1951, but the 2022 edition yielded six medals with no gold, leaving the 2026 Aichi-Nagoya campaign as a chance to close unfinished business. An 18-strong squad chosen after May 30–31 trials was pruned to 15 after Deepanshu, Mukul Dahiya and Deepak tested positive for doping, though expectations remain high across men’s freestyle, women’s freestyle and Greco-Roman categories.

items.headline: ASIAD-BOUND NEPAL BOXERS GET SAI SUPPORT TO TRAIN IN GUWAHATI
items.gist: The Sports Authority of India is hosting Nepal’s seven-member boxing team and two coaches at its Guwahati National Centre of Excellence since August 10 for joint training and sparring with Indian boxers ahead of the Asian Games. The camp, which continues till September 15 before the squad heads to Japan where competition starts September 19, has continued despite flash floods in Nepal, with SAI executive director DK Mittal calling it valuable exposure for Nepalese boxers.

items.headline: Mind in your hands
items.gist: Across urban India, exhausted professionals are turning to pottery, painting and other hands-on workshops for stress relief, with Callipottery founder Pradip and Bengaluru potter Apurva Chavan citing clay’s ego-dismantling effect and a 2026 Frontiers in Human Neuroscience scoping review linking art-making to lower cortisol — including a Drexel trial cutting average cortisol from ~17.9 to ~14.8 nmol/L in 45 minutes. Therapists and studio founders in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Bhopal and Gurugram report reduced anxiety, new friendships, and dismantled perfectionism, while Bangalore Theatre Company’s Arjun Kabbina notes creative activity can act as a stressbuster without replacing clinical treatment.

items.headline: The case for making things
items.gist: A sidebar notes that systematic reviews of craft and handmade activities — including a 2025 review of 19 craft-intervention studies and a 2024 review of 181 handmade-activity studies — associate hands-on making with better mood, lower stress, greater self-esteem, and stronger purpose. Working with clay, knitting or learning instruments demands attention and yields visible progress, challenging the brain with unfamiliar tasks in a world of passive digital consumption.

items.headline: Politics of belonging
items.gist: Rahul Singh reviews Aruni Kashyap’s *How To Date A Fanatic* (Fourth Estate, pp 368, Rs 599), a novel expanding his 2020 Boston Review story about Delhi University assistant professor Rohit navigating queer desire, Assam roots, and a post-2014 authoritarian shift across Delhi, Assam and Haryana’s private-university belt. Singh praises Kashyap’s poetic political portrait of urban-rural porosity, reservation politics, and claustrophobic luxury amid campus change, and calls Minti the character who most haunts the reader after the book ends.

items.headline: Hunt for selfhood amid daily chaos
items.gist: Aleksandra Bogdanova reviews Herta Müller’s *Traveling on One Leg* (Aleph, pp 154, Rs 599), a semi-autobiographical novel following Romanian-German Irene’s exile, loneliness, and failed romances after leaving Nicolae Ceausescu’s dictatorship for Germany. Bogdanova highlights Müller’s non-linear style, recurring water-mirror-window imagery, and Irene’s messy search for identity without marriage, career or neat resolution.

items.headline: A comic lens to perceive the world
items.gist: Anjali Chauhan reviews *The Bare Bones Book of Humour* edited by Ankit Raj Ojha (Bare Bones Pubn, Rs 199), an anthology of 24 writers from eight countries arguing humour exposes vanity, power and everyday absurdity rather than offering escape. Chauhan singles out Merlin Flower’s feminist satire *Robes and Roles* and Aparna Kalra’s *Protection*, set against Uttarakhand’s Uniform Civil Code live-in registration rules, as politically incisive examples of comedy as dissent.

items.headline: September is a month of thresholds: these three novels turn that transitional mood into stories of reunion, warmth and longing.
items.gist: Speed Reads surveys three September-set novels: Rosamunde Pilcher’s *September* reuniting MacNichol family and friends in the Scottish Highlands; Carissa Orlando’s haunted-house tale *The September House*; and Donna Tartt’s 1992 campus classic *The Secret History*, whose New England autumn atmosphere frames a privileged student group’s unraveling.

items.headline: Read of the Week
items.gist: The column highlights Francis Fukuyama’s political memoir tracing his break from neoconservative mentors after the 2003 Iraq invasion and 2008 financial crash, alongside his father’s civil rights work and CIA contract research in the 1980s. It frames the book as an urgent study of how the West can recover democracy amid shifts from Bush through Obama to Trump and Russia’s Ukraine invasion.

items.headline: A city of contrasts
items.gist: Pallabi Dey Purkayastha’s 48-hour Bhopal guide covers Upper Lake at dawn, Qudsia Begum’s 1820 Gohar Mahal, 1830 Shaukat Mahal, Shah Jahan Begum’s Taj-ul-Masajid, Bharat Bhavan’s performing arts, Chowk Bazaar street food and zardosi shopping, plus day-two trips to Sanchi Stupa, Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Manav Sangrahalaya’s tribal architecture displays, Van Vihar National Park, and a sunset boat ride before departing from Raja Bhoj Airport.

items.headline: A kadubu by any other name…
items.gist: Origin Story traces the sweet dumpling known as kadubu, kudumu, kozhukatta, modak and, in Goa, Mangaluru and coastal Karnataka, fried neureo or nevri, from Sanskrit *moda-ka* (“that which delights”) through Vedic honey fillings, Buddhist-period jaggery, Someshwara III’s *Manasollasa*, and global parallels such as pierogi and tangyuan. Food historian K T Achaya links modaka to medical “sweet uncooked pills” in Charaka and Sushrutha, while Barbara Gallani notes independent dumpling traditions spread through travel and trade.

items.headline: Culinary trail across time zones
items.gist: Ruth Dsouza Prabhu reports that beyond Ajanta-Ellora at Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, food now shapes travel through Dhyaana Farms’ curated farm meals, Chef Mohib Farooqui’s eight-seater Accentuate Food Lab tasting menus of nine to thirteen themed courses, street stops such as Hira Pao Bhaji and Mathura Wala, paan rituals, Jama Khan Mandi and Mustafa Biryani, and local staples including naan qalia, Aurangabad kantakki, tikiya pao, samosa rice and imarti.

items.headline: Truth about remission
items.gist: Dr R Shrikanth, a Hubli hemato-oncologist, explains that leukaemia “complete remission” means no detectable disease on standard tests, not guaranteed eradication of all malignant cells, with measurable residual disease (MRD) offering earlier relapse signals. He cites 2025 AML studies showing 49.7% five-year relapse among transplant patients with detectable leukaemia stem cells versus 8.5% without, and notes newer options including targeted therapy, immunotherapy and pre-emptive azacitidine when MRD turns positive.

items.headline: Multivitamins: Yes or no?
items.gist: Mythbuster examines mixed evidence on daily multivitamins, citing a 2026 Columbia University *Nature Medicine* study finding a minor biological-ageing slowdown alongside a 2024 JAMA Network Open study of 4,00,000 US adults over two decades showing no mortality benefit. It advises healthy adults to prioritise balanced food and sun exposure, follow doctor-prescribed supplementation for deficiencies, and avoid overdosing rather than taking pills “on autopilot.”

items.headline: How lapis lazuli coloured the world
items.gist: Shrey Maurya’s Discover Indian Art column traces lapis lazuli from Afghanistan’s Sar-e-Sang mines — nearly the world’s sole source until around 1950 — along Silk Road trade routes into Indus Valley beadwork from 2600 BCE, Buddhist cave pigments, Persian and Indian manuscript ateliers, and European ultramarine used by Leonardo da Vinci, Vermeer and others until 19th-century synthetics. Archaeological and museum evidence shows the stone prized for colour and supposed spiritual protection across Egypt, Nepal and beyond.

items.headline: CRACKER of a TRACKER
items.gist: Triumph's Tracker 400, India's first production street-tracker inspired by flat-track racing, pairs a Thruxton-tuned 349-cc single with a 13-litre tank, 805-mm seat, quick-shifter and firm suspension suited to tarmac rather than off-road use. A test ride on Pune's outskirts found strong braking, predictable dual-purpose tyre grip even in rain, and agile cornering from the shortest wheelbase in Triumph's 400 range.

items.headline: e-Access à la mode
items.gist: Suzuki's e-Access electric scooter offers Ride Mode B alongside Eco and Ride A, delivering about 76 km range versus Ride A's 59 km and Eco's 87 km through progressive throttle and relaxed regen suited to Indian commuting. A test run home with under 50% battery maintained 45-50 km/h and arrived with about 20 km and 20% charge remaining.

items.headline: UNDERSTANDING EARLY FACIAL Wrinkles: Causes and prevention strategies
items.gist: Premature facial wrinkles are driven largely by photoaging from UV exposure accounting for up to 80% of visible aging, plus dehydration, repetitive expressions, glycation from refined sugar, smoking, pollution, stress and poor sleep. Prevention includes daily SPF 30+ sunscreen, retinoids, vitamin C, barrier-repair moisturisers, hydration, silk pillowcases, anti-inflammatory diet and 7-9 hours of sleep, with dermatologist consultation advised for persistent concerns.

items.headline: A PAINLESS LUMP IS NOT ALWAYS HARMLESS Doctors decode the silent signs of sarcoma
items.gist: Doctors warn that painless lumps that keep growing, feel firm or fixed, exceed about 5 cm or recur after removal need evaluation because they may signal sarcoma in muscle, fat, nerves or bone. Diagnosis involves examination, ultrasound or MRI and core-needle biopsy, with surgery often central and radiation, chemotherapy or immunotherapy considered at specialist centres.

items.headline: Amid climate change, more Brits ditch tea for ice cream
items.gist: Britain's tea consumption is wilting as climate change drives record heat, with Associated British Foods reporting dampened demand for hot beverages at Twinings and Ovaltine as temperatures rose as high as 38°C during western Europe's hottest summer on record, including 40 days above 30°C in the UK. Retailers from Dunelm to RevolutionRace cited heat-driven high-street declines, while Currys benefited from cooling-appliance sales and Magnum Ice Cream reported higher-than-expected growth in July.

items.headline: All rice! An old drinking grain finds new spirit
items.gist: Indian distillers are turning heirloom rice—from Handia and Judima traditions to ukdo, chak hao, ambemohar and Basmati—into beer, whisky, gin and vodka. Diageo’s Epitome Reserve (2021) was a 100% rice whisky; Mysuru’s Huli now makes “rice malt” whisky from malted local paddy, producing about 70,000 bottles a year after four years of R&D.
items.paragraph: Indian distillers are turning heirloom rice—from Handia and Judima traditions to ukdo, chak hao, ambemohar and Basmati—into beer, whisky, gin and vodka. Diageo’s Epitome Reserve (2021) was a 100% rice whisky; Mysuru’s Huli now makes “rice malt” whisky from malted local paddy, producing about 70,000 bottles a year after four years of R&D. Goa Brewing Company builds 95% of its beer on rice, sourcing from ~180 farming families at 25% above MSP; last year unseasonal rain wiped out nearly 90% of crop in some Goa talukas. Smoke Lab’s Basmati-based vodka has sold over 150,000 cases in the US; Jin Jiji gin from Kumaon rice is poured at top US bars.

items.headline: Finding our way home may be the final frontier
items.gist: On Star Trek’s 60th anniversary, Jai Arjun Singh recalls discovering the series’ colour via a US-returned aunt’s videocassette after watching it in black-and-white on Doordarshan in the mid-1980s, and how Kirk, Spock and the Enterprise crew shaped a generation of Indian viewers. He notes later iterations including Next Generation’s gender-neutral “where no one has gone before,” and cites astronauts Swati Mohan and Sirisha Bandla crediting Star Trek for their space careers.

items.headline: Walls take a curve
items.gist: Curved walls are moving from furniture accents into luxury interior architecture, with designers using aluminium framing, flexi-ply and MDF finished in paint or stone to soften straight lines in living rooms and passageways. Experts say curves work best to define zones in open plans or guide movement in corridors, pair well with sculptural lighting and statement art rather than competing decor, and demand skilled craftsmanship—though overly tight curves or too many rounded elements can overwhelm a space.

items.headline: FORGET CELEBRITIES, ASK THE ATHLETE
items.gist: A Business of Fashion Insights report on fashion and sports e-commerce finds athletes are the most trusted public figures for product recommendations, with almost a third of consumers likely to act on their advice compared with 17% for celebrities and macro-influencers and 19% for micro-influencers. The survey suggests influence is shifting from scale to specificity, even as 73% of consumers say friends and family remain the strongest purchase drivers.

items.headline: COST PER WEAR: FASHION'S NEW ECONOMIC MODEL
items.gist: Cost per wear divides a garment’s price by expected wears, and research by the University of Bath and Cambridge Judge Business School published in Psychology & Marketing found shoppers shown CPW figures were more likely to choose pricier, higher-quality items over cheaper alternatives. Applied like supermarket unit pricing, a CPW label could make a ₹15,000 long-lasting coat look different from a ₹3,000 piece needing frequent replacement, signalling a shift from upfront price to value per wear that luxury brands emphasizing craftsmanship may benefit from most.

items.headline: Cluttercore is bringing soul back to homes
items.gist: After years of minimal interiors, cluttercore is celebrating meaningful accumulation—layering books, art, ceramics, photographs and vintage finds to create personal, lived-in spaces rather than random clutter. Designers quoted in The Spruce and House Beautiful say curated collections with breathing space, grouped objects and varied heights add warmth and character, with Pinterest’s 2026 Hobbies Trend Report highlighting “Curated Clutter” as homeowners seek tactile, expressive rooms built around micro-collections that tell their story.

items.headline: How to: Add millet to your daily meals
items.gist: Mix cooked millets 50/50 with rice for grain bowls, or swap a quarter of regular flour with ragi or jowar when baking. Keep foxtail millet to replace rice and ragi flour for breakfast; use whole sorghum or pearl millet for salads and soups.
items.paragraph: Mix cooked millets 50/50 with rice for grain bowls, or swap a quarter of regular flour with ragi or jowar when baking. Keep foxtail millet to replace rice and ragi flour for breakfast; use whole sorghum or pearl millet for salads and soups. Soak grains for 4 to 6 hours before cooking, and dry-roast raw millet for 3 minutes for a nutty flavour. Build habits with ragi porridge at breakfast, millet in lunch salads, khichdi for dinner, and puffed millets as a snack.

items.headline: Wakey, wakey
items.gist: The human body's circadian rhythm, governed by the suprachiasmatic nucleus in the brain, prepares the body for wakefulness in the hours before a habitual waking time through rising stress hormone levels and increasing body temperature. Waking a few minutes before an alarm can reflect this learned cycle rather than pure coincidence or foresight, as people tend to remember uncanny successes like waking seconds before the alarm and forget mornings when they woke much earlier for no apparent reason.

items.gist: Ameesha Patel’s parents’ Churchgate home in Mumbai was allegedly burgled, with gold and diamond jewellery worth around ₹5 lakh reported missing. Police have arrested a 40-year-old domestic help who had worked at Ameesha’s mother Asha Patel’s residence for nearly 1.5 years, and the court remanded her to police custody until September 15.

items.headline: I'm glad he accepted the invitation, says Ajith on Vijay flagging off Le Mans race
items.gist: Actor-racer Ajith Kumar welcomed Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay flagging off Round 5 of the 2026 Michelin Le Mans Cup at Silverstone on September 12, thanking him for visiting despite a busy schedule after 34 years as colleagues in the film industry. Ajith said he was glad Vijay accepted the invitation to assess what it would take for Chennai to host events like the Le Mans series, noting the state government’s broader push to promote sports beyond motorsport.

items.headline: I'm in a zone now where I want to be more present in every moment: Saif
items.gist: Saif Ali Khan, speaking as Haiwaan plays in theatres and a Bombay Times Lounge episode goes live, said he wants to balance life well, do good work and be more present in every moment rather than let stardom distract from what matters. He reflected on staying grounded, valuing criticism and creating screen moments that are remembered, adding that a handful of good films can make a career worthwhile even if not every project registers as hoped.

items.headline: Women lose screen space, but gain Emmy spotlight
items.gist: Female representation declined across the 2025–26 US television season even as women creators punched above their weight among Emmy nominees, a Center for the Study of Women in Television and Film at San Diego State University study found. Female creators on streaming fell from 36% to 24%, major female characters dropped to 44% of speaking roles, yet women accounted for 31% of nominated comedy and drama shows despite making up only about 22% of creators, and female directors received 42% of Outstanding Director nominations in those categories despite comprising 20% of directors.

items.headline: BRICS leaders seek stronger cooperation over AI safety
items.gist: BRICS leaders on Saturday called for wider access to AI resources and stronger international cooperation to ensure the technology is safe, secure, inclusive and reliable, committing to implement the grouping's statement on "Global Governance of artificial intelligence". The New Delhi Declaration 2026 laid out a broad technology agenda spanning AI, cybersecurity, digital public infrastructure, telecom, submarine networks, quantum technologies, startups and advanced manufacturing, and pushed for concerted efforts to address digital security threats, foster AI for science and innovation, develop trustworthy AI technologies and improve energy efficiency of AI systems.

items.headline: Being a woman, living in a world of fear
items.gist: Globally one in three women has experienced physical or sexual violence per UN estimates, and India reported over 4 lakh crimes against women in 2024—over 1,200 daily per NCRB—as deep-rooted patriarchy and India’s rank of 131 of 148 on the Global Gender Gap Index 2025 compound unsafe public transport, workplaces and digital spaces. A 2025 LinkedIn survey found about 70% of Indian corporate women experienced workplace harassment, with many not reporting for fear of retaliation and willing to forgo 19% of wages for safer workplaces; cybercrimes against women rose 239% between 2017 and 2022 per a Joint Parliamentary Committee report, while legal safeguards including BNS sections and the POSH Act face gaps in street-harassment coverage, police sensitisation, digital-law enforcement and low conviction rates that discourage complaints.

items.headline: PM urges BRICS leaders to draw up 10 global governance reform proposals
items.gist: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday made a strong pitch for global reform, highlighting the imbalance between decision-makers and those impacted by their decisions, and called for BRICS to transition from "rule-takers to rule-shapers". He proposed that leaders at the 18th BRICS Summit arrive at 10 proposals for global governance reform to develop into a BRICS Reform Road map, a BRICS Continuity and Implementation Mechanism for the Troika to follow up on initiatives, and a secure digital repository tracking nodal points, deadlines and implementation status.
items.paragraph: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday made a strong pitch for global reform, highlighting the imbalance between decision-makers and those impacted by their decisions, and called for BRICS to transition from "rule-takers to rule-shapers". He proposed that leaders at the 18th BRICS Summit arrive at 10 proposals for global governance reform to develop into a BRICS Reform Road map, a BRICS Continuity and Implementation Mechanism for the Troika to follow up on initiatives, and a secure digital repository tracking nodal points, deadlines and implementation status. Mr. Modi stressed reform of the UN Security Council with text-based negotiations linked to a definite timeline, voting power and leadership positions in financial institutions reflecting today's economic realities, a Seafarers' Emergency Support Network, and transforming the Global South from rule-takers into rule-shapers in AI, cyberspace, outer space and biotechnology.

items.headline: Going 1980s? Police, experts red-flag retro avatar trend
items.gist: Bengaluru police and cybersecurity experts have warned citizens against uploading high-quality selfies to unregulated third-party apps for Instagram's 1980s AI photo trend, saying such apps can harvest biometric data for facial recognition, deepfakes, identity theft and scams. DCP (crime) Imam Raja Kasim said miscreants use AI-generated images of others as display pictures to impersonate reputed persons and lure victims into sharing personal or financial data, sometimes obtaining banking credentials; police have spread warnings through posters and social media and advised using verified platforms, stripping EXIF metadata and turning off AI model training.

items.paragraph: At a panel on 'Tulu Wikipedia in the age of AI' during the 10th anniversary celebrations in Mangaluru on Saturday, Wikimedians said artificial intelligence is not a threat to Wikipedia if content is thoroughly verified, filtered, edited and used. Senior IT expert and Kannada and Tulu Wikipedia admin U.B. items.headline: AI can do the work, can students do the thinking?
items.gist: Agentic AI reshapes learning and hiring by taking a goal, breaking it into steps, choosing tools, executing and checking results, unlike ordinary chatbots that only answer questions. Nearly half of ChatGPT’s Indian users are under 24 and use it for studying, while a PNAS randomised trial found school students with unrestricted GPT-4 access scored 48% better on practice problems but 17% worse on unaided exams when the tool was withdrawn.

Nearly half of ChatGPT’s Indian users are under 24 and use it for studying, while a PNAS randomised trial found school students with unrestricted GPT-4 access scored 48% better on practice problems but 17% worse on unaided exams when the tool was withdrawn. The piece warns of metacognitive offloading, false confidence from flawless AI output, and a labour-market mismatch as Indian IT fresher hiring fell from about 6 lakh in FY 2022 to about 1.2 lakh in FY 2025 even as employability rates rose.

items.headline: Saudis shut key pipeline after attack, spark fears of further fuel price rise
items.gist: Saudi Arabia temporarily shut its 1,200km East-West pipeline as a precaution after a drone attack that both Baghdad and Riyadh said originated in Iraq, where Iranian-backed militias operate; Iraq dismissed a commander on Saturday after the strike. The pipeline has moved 4 million to 5 million barrels per day—4% to 5% of global supply—serving as the main West Asian oil export route while the Strait of Hormuz has been largely shut by war, and satellite images showed black smoke rising south of Medina.

items.headline: Why is NCPCR investigating Meta, Instagram?
items.gist: Following a BBC investigation that found Instagram running paid advertisements promoting child sexual exploitation and abuse material in India, the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights summoned Meta officials for a hearing on September 9 and the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology also summoned the company. Automatic moderation systems and AI detection cannot catch every violative submission, and the Tech Transparency Project reported that Meta sometimes classified removed CSEAM ads as adult sexual content and rejected 57% of reported CSEAM ads as not violating Advertising Standards.

items.headline: Anthropic says UAE-linked AI op targeted UN staff over Sudan
items.gist: AI firm Anthropic said it detected and disrupted a UAE-linked influence operation that targeted the Muslim Brotherhood and United Nations experts critical of Abu Dhabi's alleged role in Sudan's war, linking the campaign "with high confidence" to UAE government officials. Using Anthropic's Claude chatbot, the operation generated reports, advocacy materials, social media content and testimony on Sudan, compiled "counter-accountability dossiers" on UN special rapporteurs who criticised the UAE, and appropriated the identity of a Sudanese human rights organisation to draft testimony for named individuals.

items.headline: Let outsiders evaluate AI safety: Anthropic chief
items.gist: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for all frontier AI companies to give "ongoing, employee-like access" to outside evaluators to monitor safety practices, days after Anthropic blocked malicious uses of its models and following OpenAI's report of an AI system hacking another AI company in July. Amodei also urged democratic governments to coordinate with authoritarian ones so rivals do not accelerate when US firms intentionally pace development, as researcher resignations from Anthropic's safety team underscored industry tensions over responsible AI deployment.

items.headline: Tolstoy's influence on Gandhi had a more profound impact than his books
items.gist: Daniil Tolstoy, Leo Tolstoy's great-grandson, and Gopalkrishna Gandhi, Mahatma Gandhi's grandson, have revisited the century-old correspondence between their ancestors in 'Truth and Love: The Gandhi-Tolstoy Letters', with Daniil telling Sneha Bhura that although the seven letters exchanged in 1909–10 are known in scholarly circles, the wider public is largely unaware of the close connection, and that Tolstoy's influence on Gandhi — drawn to the moral radical behind 'The Kingdom of God Is Within You' rather than the novelist of 'War and Peace' — had a more profound impact on the world than his literature. Daniil, an academic and organic farmer whose family fled Russia after the 1917 Revolution and who is now cut off from his farm there because of the war, argues that in an era of algorithmic control, ecological collapse and militarised conflict, their ideas remind us that genuine survival depends on human conscience choosing truth and non-violence over brute force.

items.headline: Brics AI plan leaves question of jobs largely unanswered
items.gist: The BRICS New Delhi Declaration sets an ambitious plan to prepare people for an AI-driven economy but largely sidesteps what happens to workers whose jobs are lost or sharply changed by automation and AI. It frames AI as an opportunity for growth and sustainable development while stressing safety, security, inclusion and reliability, and commits members to forecasting skills needs by analysing labour-market trends in digital, green, care and other priority sectors—rather than spelling out protections when technology replaces existing work.

items.headline: AI formalises Fermat's Last Theorem proof in 11 days
items.gist: Anthropic has used its Claude AI to formalise Fermat's Last Theorem using the Lean language, translating human arguments into code so software can verify every logical step from first principles without relying on human trust. While mathematicians had anticipated the translation would take five years of painstaking work, Claude achieved it in 11 days, generating over 13 million lines of code and verifying 29,500 intermediate theorems in a breakthrough for automated reasoning.

items.headline: BRICS supplies 42% of India's imports, buys only 22% of its exports (Opinion)
items.gist: Ajay Srivastava writes India's BRICS goods trade rose from $203 billion in FY2021 to $417.5 billion in FY2026 as imports jumped 131.8% to $321.8 billion while exports grew 48.8% to $95.7 billion, tripling the deficit to $226.1 billion. items.headline: Germany’s far-right movement is no longer on the fringe (Opinion)
items.gist: Alternative for Germany won about 44% and 39 of 83 seats in Saxony-Anhalt state elections, more than doubling its prior support while Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s CDU fell to 17.2% and 15 seats with about 78% turnout—the AfD’s best result though three seats short of a majority. The outcome pressures Merz ahead of Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania polls, emboldens Europe’s far right, and raises questions about sustaining the political firewall isolating the AfD as it leads national polls at about 28% with policies on migration, energy, Ukraine and Russia complicating European integration and ReArm Europe defence plans.

items.headline: Why India's schools should take note of New York's AI ban
items.gist: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Schools Chancellor Kamar H. Samuels unveiled sweeping curbs on AI use and screen time in the city's public schools on September 2, barring student-facing AI tools for kindergarten through eighth grade for a year and imposing age-calibrated screen time limits affecting over 600,000 students.

John Xavier argues India should pay close attention as ASER's 2024 survey found 82.2% of children aged 14-16 know how to operate a smartphone but only a little over half use it for anything educational, with India's device deficit in schools potentially a blessing if paired with age-tiered policies, evaluation mechanisms, and attention to smartphone use at home rather than waiting for a crisis.

items.gist: Apropos of 'No, GDP data…' (ATM, Sept 6), Sanjay Chopra of Mohali writes that growth numbers warrant cautious interpretation because the war has created fiscal pressures and increased the subsidy burden, and India must focus on structural growth drivers — particularly manufacturing, exports, investment and productivity — to sustain high growth.

items.headline: How Brics went from supporting actor to main-character energy (Opinion)
items.gist: Daulet Singh argues that a decade ago Brics was seen as a supporting actor in US-led order-building, but the US has become a spoiler through weaponisation of public goods, and Brics is now the only multilateral institution upholding interconnections between diverse economies without geopolitical overhang — with intra-Brics trade expanding over 13 times in two decades while intra-G-7 trade only doubled, and Brics+ share of world merchandise imports rising from 11% in 2000 to 17% by 2025 as G-7's share fell from 45% to 25%. He writes that Brics must avoid becoming an eloquent talk shop and squandering a unique window to advance multipolarisation, with China and India obliged to cushion the world economy and supply public goods while frontline members like Iran resist aggression, and notes Xi and Modi are demonstrating that India-China differences will not prevent them from steering the multipolar age positively.

items.headline: China's X factor, and why India needs its own narrative (Opinion)
items.gist: Former ambassador Ashok K Kantha writes that Xi Jinping's 2013 call to "tell China's story well" has spawned a large institutional ecosystem for "discourse power," including well-funded think-tanks and quasi-private bodies, but Chinese transgressions in eastern Ladakh and Galwan in 2020 broke the pattern of India-China Think-Tanks Forum meetings almost overnight. He notes that despite more calibrated outreach — including Chinese scholars building followings on X, advertorials on Tibet, and journalist fellowships — Pew's modest global warming toward China in 2025–2026 barely touched India, where America is still favoured, and argues no amount of nimble messaging will improve how China is seen in India as long as it treats India as a lesser power expected to defer rather than a peer civilisation with its own agency, while India should build its own narrative in China using organic assets such as accounting for at least 10% of China's record trade surplus last year and Buddhism's birthplace status.

items.headline: What the cute orangutans reveal about our 'ugly' biases (Opinion)
items.gist: Environment journalist Bahar Dutt writes that orangutans arriving on India's coastline made national headlines as "SO cute" but are victims of an international crime network, and since Indonesia has formally requested their return India should repatriate them under CITES once origin is confirmed — while noting a UN Environment report found over 70,000 native and exotic live animals and derivatives trafficked through 18 Indian airports between 2011 and 2020, with reptiles accounting for 46% of seizures yet rarely eliciting sympathy. She urges the environment minister to expedite repatriation, customs to explain how live animals entered through India's coast, and consumers to examine palm-oil presence in products, noting ICAR has identified over 133,000 hectares in Arunachal Pradesh as suitable for palm oil cultivation, raising deforestation concerns, and that every reptile or "ugly" animal seized in the wildlife trade also deserves dignity instead of languishing in rescue centres.

items.headline: Houthis may put world in dire straits over diesel (Opinion)
items.gist: Swaminathan S Anklesaria Aiyar writes that Houthis capturing Mocha port and islands controlling Bab el-Mandeb — through which 9.3 mbd of oil and petroleum products passed before 2023 attacks halved flows to 4.6 mbd by 2025 — may create a disastrous shortage of refined products especially diesel, with Brent crude already rising from $90/barrel to $105/barrel and US retail diesel crossing $6/gallon and possibly hitting $8/gallon, double its price at the year's start. He notes Saudi Arabia diverted exports through its East-West pipeline to the Red Sea reaching 8.1 mbd in the April–June quarter after Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz in April 2026, but Houthis attacking Saudi cities and refineries have now shut down production, Trump twice declined MBS's personal appeals for US military action despite a Nov Strategic Defense Agreement, and if both Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb remain closed India's oil subsidy bill could go through the roof despite soaring refinery profits as refined product prices outpace crude.

items.headline: Persons of forest, prisoners of men: How orangutans turn up in India (Opinion)
items.gist: Five baby orangutans seized in Odisha highlight illegal wildlife trade from their native Malaysia and Indonesia range, likely driven by demand for private exotic menageries rather than kinship with humans who share nearly 97% of their DNA. Ecologist Seshadri K S argues the infants were probably snatched from killed mothers, that India’s CITES enforcement through the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau on a Rs 13 crore budget is overstretched, and that the five orphans should be repatriated to semi-wild settings in their home range rather than kept in zoos or private rescue centres.

items.headline: Police station footage: Seen and unseen (Opinion)
items.gist: Venkatesh Nayak contrasts recent pro-accountability judicial signals with an Allahabad High Court order upholding denial of RTI access to police-station CCTV footage under Section 8(1)(g), limiting release to courts or human rights commissions only after a complaint. He notes mandatory CCTV under the Supreme Court’s 2020 Paramvir Singh Saini directions, Karnataka Information Commission penalties of Rs 15,000-25,000 on three Kalaburagi police officers for non-compliance, and argues footage should not become a “sarkari secret” when citizens lawfully record police interactions.

items.headline: BRICS raises the reform pitch (Opinion)
items.gist: Srikanth Kondapalli writes that the 18th BRICS Summit’s 140-paragraph New Delhi Declaration pushes multipolarity, UN/UNSC/IMF reform, and Global South leadership while treading cautiously on West Asia and omitting de-dollarisation despite nearly half of $1.1 trillion intra-BRICS trade settling in renminbi. The declaration condemned the 2025 Pahalgam attack that killed 26 people, backed the New Development Bank, and called for reliable critical-mineral supply chains amid tariff and sanctions disruptions.

items.headline: And some dance just to move (Opinion)
items.gist: S R Ramakrishna argues dance fitness has democratised movement across Indian cities, with gym-chain memberships costing Rs 50-80 a day drawing mixed-age groups to secular, non-judgmental sessions set to pan-Indian playlists. Citing Basavanna’s jangama ideal in a modern key, he contrasts costly formal dance training with accessible hourly classes that offer community, step counts, and physical relief without guru-shishya commitment.

items.headline: Information, truth and connection in the AI age (Opinion)
items.gist: Gopichand Katragadda responds to Yuval Noah Harari by defining information as data with sufficient context to reduce uncertainty for a given purpose, not inherently truth-bearing connection. He warns that generative AI makes fluent falsehood cheap, urges readers to verify primary sources and treat AI answers as leads, and argues societies must distinguish data, belief, and truth rather than confuse political narrative with statistical analysis.
